sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Stribog** ​(*stribog*) — ‌Winds, ‌Storms · ​Father of ​winds ​— belongs ​to ​the Slavic ‌tradition, ​where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Winds, ​Storms". The ‌name ​means "Father ​of ​winds"[^1].

**Stribog** ​is ​the wind-god ‌of the ​Kyiv ‌pantheon, sixth ​of ‌the six ​idols ‌cast into ​the ‌Dnieper in 988. ​His name's ​second ‌element is ‌the ‌word for ​'god'; ​its first ‌is ​opaque — ​but the ‌epic ​tradition calls ​the ‌winds his ​grandsons, ‌and that ​one ​formula is ​the whole ​of ‌his surviving ‌theology.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling ‌**Stribog** and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/stribog/). ‌The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *stribog* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Stribog** is ​a ​scholarly transliteration ‌of ​the ​reconstructed spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically the ‌name ​means "Father ‌of ​winds"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Stribog** matches ​the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*stribog* contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ​lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. ​The editorial ‌work ​is to ​fix ‌one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ​the ​original evidence ​visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ‌from ‌the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **s** ​→ ​**S** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ​**t** → ​**t** ‌— Same
- ​**r** ​→ ​**r** — ‌Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ​— Same
- ‌**b** ​→ ‌**b** — ‌Same
- ​**o** → ​**o** ​— Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ‌**g** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/stribog/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**stribog** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Stribog.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Stribog" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Stribog" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"stribog" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Stribog ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Stribog ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Stribog ‌place ​winds, storms ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Stribog appears ‌in ​slavic ‌tradition as ​winds, ​storms. The ​name's ​meaning, ​"Father of ‌winds", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ‌Stribog in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Stribog ​survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ‌Each ​version reflects ​the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Stribog ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Stribog ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Stribog, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​winds ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Stribog ​is the ‌god of ‌what passes ​through. Wind ​cannot be ​sworn by, ​cannot be ​fed, cannot ‌even be ​consistently blamed ​— and ‌so the ​tradition left ‌him almost ​nothing ‌to hold. ​What the ​epic gives ​him instead ​is better ​than a ‌cult: a ​family. The ‌winds are ​his grandsons ‌— not ​his subjects, ‌not his ​weapons, ‌his grandsons, ​the way ​weather actually ‌behaves, arriving ‌uninvited, full ‌of intentions, ​unmistakably related. ​The phrase ‌is a ​miniature of ​how polytheism ‌worked before ​it learned ​to be ‌systematic: ​the world ‌is not ​governed, it ​is inhabited, ​by beings ​with kin. ‌Stribog matters ‌to the ​modern imagination ‌precisely because ​he is ​so nearly ‌empty — ‌a vessel ‌into ‌which every ​age pours ‌its theory ​of the ​wind, from ​philology's unsolved ‌root to ​fantasy's storm ​lord. Perhaps ​a god ‌who is ​only a ​name and ​a ‌family of ​winds is ‌the truest ​wind-god of ‌all: felt ​everywhere, pinned ‌down nowhere, ‌and quoted ​— 'the ​winds, Stribog's ​grandsons' — ​whenever the ‌air itself ‌needs a ​lineage.[^1]
